title: promptset-coverage-heatmap-and-regression-journal
content:
Purpose
This is a working journal documenting an empirical probe into how low-precision deploys (int8, int4, AWQ, GPTQ) affect quality across our onboarding prompt sets. The framing is practical: surface slices that break, estimate unit economics tradeoffs, and recommend targeted mitigations rather than blanket reverts. Notes here are informal; numbers are exploratory but reproducible via the linked harness.

Executive summary (TL;DR)
- Baseline (fp16) -> reference. We ran the QA/Instruction/Code/Conversational prompt sets used for onboarding candidate models against four quant variants: int8 (calibrated), AWQ-int4, GPTQ-int4 (per-layer), and int8+KV-cache-lite.
- Most slices tolerate int8 with median metric delta ~ -0.6% (relative).
- AWQ-int4 shows concentrated failures in 3 slice families (constraint-following, numeric reasoning with long context, and tokenizer-edge code snippets) with deltas ranging -4% to -18% depending on metric and slice.
- GPTQ-int4 exhibited milder but broader degradation vs AWQ on instruction-following and factual QA; error modes are different (hallucination style vs nonsense tokenization).
- Actionable outcome: mark two prompt-set slices as "int4-sensitive" and route those requests to int8 or fp16 in experiment; apply targeted post-quantization calibration for AWQ for the top-2 failure patterns.

Quick methodology notes
- Prompt sets: a stratified sample across onboarding corpus: instruction-flows (450 prompts), code-snippets (320), multi-turn convo (520), closed-book QA (600), math/arith puzzles (280). Each prompt has canonical reference and multiple acceptable responses where applicable.
- Metrics: for closed QA we use exact-match and token-level chrF; for instruction-following we use an annotator-derived utility score (0-100) averaged then normalized to percent; for code we use unit-test pass rate where applicable and whitespace-agnostic string-match otherwise; for convos we use BLEU + annotator coherence score.
- Platforms: baseline = fp16 on xG A100; int8 = dynamic-range calibrated int8 build (our standard). AWQ-int4 and GPTQ-int4 were generated via the quant-harness branch noted above. Each variant served on identical container configs with warm cache.
- Run cadence: 3 seeds (random batching) x full prompt sweep; report median and 90% CI.

Coverage heatmap concept (how we slice)
We created a 2D categorical coverage grid: difficulty (easy / moderate / adversarial) vs content type (QA / instruction / code / multi-turn / math). Each cell ~100-400 examples depending on availability. Heatmap score = relative drop vs baseline (negative is worse). We then drill down top 20% worst examples in each cell to label failure modes (tokenization, instruction-drift, hallucination, timeout/truncation).

Representative per-slice deltas (median, relative to fp16)
- QA - closed-book - easy: int8 -0.3%, AWQ-int4 -1.7%, GPTQ-int4 -1.1%
- QA - closed-book - adversarial (paraphrase+negation): int8 -1.2%, AWQ-int4 -7.4%, GPTQ-int4 -4.9%
- Instruction - short actionable tasks (moderate): int8 -0.5%, AWQ-int4 -3.8%, GPTQ-int4 -2.6%
- Instruction - constraint-heavy (e.g., "output CSV only"): int8 -0.8%, AWQ-int4 -12.2%, GPTQ-int4 -6.7%
- Code - small functions / python snippets: int8 -0.4pp unit-pass, AWQ-int4 -6.0pp unit-pass, GPTQ-int4 -3.5pp unit-pass
- Multi-turn convo - persona/context retention: int8 -0.7%, AWQ-int4 -4.0%, GPTQ-int4 -2.9%
- Math - multi-step arithmetic (long context): int8 -1.1%, AWQ-int4 -9.8%, GPTQ-int4 -5.2%

Top failure slices (names + short description)
- S1: "CSV-constraint-instructions"
  - Description: prompts that strictly require returning machine-parseable CSV-only output.
  - Failure mode: AWQ-int4 often injects filler tokens or splits separators incorrectly. Fail rate delta up to -18% (annotator utility).

- S2: "Numeric-chaining-12+-terms"
  - Description: arithmetic chains with 12+ intermediate steps or long carry operations.
  - Failure mode: rounding/precision drift at token-level causes final answer to be off; AWQ-int4 shows largest degradation.

- S3: "Tokenizer-weird-code-edges"
  - Description: short code snippets that include non-ascii punctuation + uncommon token boundaries.
  - Failure mode: GPTQ-int4 occasionally emits malformed tokens leading to syntax errors; AWQ-int4 sometimes outputs truncated lines.

- S4: "Negation-paraphrase-QA"
  - Description: QA items that hinge on a negation or subtle paraphrase change.
  - Failure mode: increased hallucination or mis-selection of evidence span. GPTQ-int4 and AWQ-int4 both show elevated error rates but AWQ more extreme.

Detailed anecdote (example trace)
Prompt: "List the three countries that do NOT border Germany, among: France, Poland, Austria, Portugal. Output CSV: country,reason"
- fp16: "Portugal, not bordering Germany" (utility 100)
- int8: same (utility 100)
- GPTQ-int4: "Portugal, does not share a border" (utility 95)
- AWQ-int4: "Portugal , France, because they don't" (malformed and wrong multi-item) (utility 42)
Notes: AWQ produced spurious extra item and separator variance; this maps to S1 and S4.

Signal inspection and possible root causes
- Token quantization sensitivity: AWQ-int4 aggressive weight quant mapping appears to amplify small logits around separators and punctuation, explaining delimiter corruption in CSV tasks.
- Long-context arithmetic instabilities: lower precision reduces effective dynamic range of intermediate accumulation, causing carry/round drift.
- GPTQ permutation/ordering artifacts: GPTQ per-layer channel quant can cause localized tokenization shifts in fringe token ids (rare tokens).

Proposed mitigations (short list, prioritized)
1) Routing policy: add slice-level routing in the serving layer — for identified S1 and S2 prompts, route to int8 or baseline. Quick win: reduce customer-visible regression without globally disabling int4.
2) AWQ post-quant calibration: run a targeted calibration pass on delimiter/punctuation tokens with a small corpus of constraint-like prompts; measure separator logit recovery. (Linked PR for harness: linked_artifacts[1]).
3) Prompt engineering guardrails: for CSV/strict-output prompts, prepend explicit canonical header tokenization hint (e.g., "---BEGIN_CSV---") and run a small post-format validator. This is cheap and often sufficient.
4) Per-slice hybrid execution: for expensive math chains, run internal verification via a deterministic small-int64 arithmetic checker on the model's output; if mismatch, re-run on int8/fp16 and use that answer.
5) Retrain-aware: flag these slices for potential fine-tuning with low-precision aware quantization-aware training (QAT) in the next onboarding stage if routing is not acceptable for product constraints.

Risk / cost notes
- Routing increases p99 latency for routed requests when falling back to fp16; quantify expected traffic: ~4.8% of onboarding prompt traffic currently maps to sensitive slices; if moved to fp16 we estimate +7% unit cost for overall workload, but reduces user-visible regressions by ~72% in current sample.
- Calibration and lightweight prompt fixes cost engineering time but minimal infra cost. QAT is highest cost but yields better long-term robustness.

Open experiments / TODOs
- [ ] Run a signer-level token logit difference analysis for AWQ vs fp16 on S1 examples (Ravi). Tracking ticket: INF-4829.
- [ ] Prototype a quick routing rule in the dev gateway that matches simple regexes for CSV-like constraints and measure false positives (Yuna).
- [ ] Re-run AWQ build with 8-bit bias correction heuristics and compare on S3 (Diego).
- [ ] Expand promptset with 2k additional adversarial paraphrases for negation tests.

Appendix: reproducibility notes
- Harness: repo/model-onboard: branch quant-coverage-journal; see linked PR for exact command line and seeds.
- Eval config used: metrics.yaml v3; sampling seed list [11, 37, 101]; batch size 16 for latency parity; warmup 50 queries.
- Raw results stored in the drive folder: shared_drives/engineering/applied-ml/quant-coverage-raw-2025-01-12 (CSV exports).

Concluding note
This doc is a snapshot of where things stand mid-onboarding. Int8 remains a strong cost/quality win; AWQ/GPTQ-int4 need methodical, slice-aware mitigation to be considered safe defaults. Recommendations above aim to preserve the cost benefits of int4 when possible while protecting high-risk slices via routing or small calibration fixes.

Signed-off-by: Ava Martinez (eng-applied-ml)
